bib.title: A comparison of Human, GPT-3.5, and GPT-4 Performance in a University-Level Coding Course

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "A comparison of Human, GPT-3.5, and GPT-4 Performance in a University-Level Coding Course" (running head "Can ChatGPT Pass a University Coding Course?"), Will Yeadon, Craig P. Testrow, Alex Peach (Durham University Physics), arXiv:2403.16977v1 [cs.CL], preprint, 25 Mar 2024.
COVERAGE: 31084 of 31084 chars, all 9 pages, including references and Appendix A (marker breakdown, ICC). Nothing skipped. Figures 1-3 are images and I did not view them. Only their captions were extracted.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- Students beat the best AI category. Student mean was 91.9% (SE 0.4) and GPT-4 with prompt engineering was 81.1% (SE 0.8).
  number: 91.9% vs 81.1%; t = -8.193; p = 2.482e-10
  setup: 14 plots, scored out of 5 each (max 70), from 8 Durham "Laboratory Skills and Electronics" Python assignments. 10 submissions per AI category, 50 student submissions, 3 blind markers, n=300 data points. GPT-4 is gpt-4-1106-preview.
  quote: "Students averaged 91.9% (SE:0.4), surpassing the highest performing AI submission category, GPT-4 with prompt engineering, which scored 81.1% (SE:0.8) - a statistically significant difference (p = 2.482 × 10−10)."
  where: abstract, p1. The t-test is in section 3.1, p4-5.
  Inconsistency: the body says "students achieved an average of 91.1%" while the abstract says 91.9%.
- Prompt engineering raised scores for both models, and the gain was far larger for the weaker model.
  number: GPT-4 71.9% (SE 1.3) to 81.1% (SE 0.8), p=1.661e-4. GPT-3.5 30.9% (SE 1.2) to 48.8% (SE 1.4), p=4.967e-9. That is +9.2 points for GPT-4 and +17.9 for GPT-3.5.
  setup: t-tests. Raw means the assignment with minimal pre-processing (Table 1). Prompt-engineered means the Table 2 rewrite. The gpt-3.5-turbo model was used for GPT-3.5. 10 submissions per category.
  quote: "GPT-4's scores increased from 71.9% (SE:1.3) to 81.1% (SE:0.8) with a p-value of 1.661 × 10−4 from a t-test, and GPT-3.5's scores improved from 30.9% (SE:1.2) to 48.8% (SE:1.4) with a t-test giving a p-value of 4.967 × 10−9."
  where: section 3.1, p5
- GPT-4 is strictly better than GPT-3.5 in both conditions. This implies that the raw GPT-4 (71.9%) beats the prompt-engineered GPT-3.5 (48.8%).
  number: 71.9% vs 48.8%
  quote: "we observed a strict superiority in the capabilities of GPT-4 over GPT-3.5"
  where: conclusion, p7
- The Mixed category (half the plots from students, half from prompt-engineered GPT-4) scored below GPT-4 alone.
  number: 76.0% (SE 1.3)
  setup: 10 mixed submissions, 14 plots each, half chosen at random with random.choice from five student entries. The authors suggest the cause is variability in the sampled student work.
  quote: "the mixed submissions, comprising both student and GPT-4 work, scored lower (76.0% with SE: 1.3) than GPT-4 submissions alone."
  where: p5
- Blind markers could identify AI work.
  number: 85.3% binary accuracy (Marker 1 89%, Marker 2 77%, Marker 3 90%). 92.1% of work rated "Definitely Human" was human-authored. 73.1% for "Probably human", 22.4% for "Probably AI", 8.4% for "Definitely AI".
  setup: 4-point Likert scale from "Definitely AI" to "Definitely Human", over 300 ratings. Mean Likert scores (AI=0 to Human=3): GPT-3.5 raw 0.033, GPT-3.5 PE 0.200, GPT-4 raw 0.467, GPT-4 PE 1.167, Mixed 1.300, Human 2.367. Cochran-Armitage p=0.025, trend 0.302.
  quote: "the reviewers managed an average accuracy rate of 85.3%, with scores of 89% for Marker #1, 77% for Marker #2, and 90% for Marker #3."
  where: abstract, section 3.2 and Fig 2 caption, p5-6
- Grader reliability was high. ICC1 and ICC2 were both 0.932. The ANOVA on the three markers' means gave F=2.72, p=0.067, so the means were not significantly different.
  setup: three markers, 100 submissions, df 99/200 (ICC1) and 99/198 (ICC2), 95% CI [0.91, 0.95] for ICC1 and [0.83, 0.97] for ICC2. Rubric is a specific marking scheme for plot quality, with runtime also mentioned.
  quote: "both ICC1 and ICC2 yielded a high value of 0.932, indicating an excellent agreement and consistency in the ratings provided by the markers."
  where: Appendix A and Table 3, p9. Note: this is a failure to reject, not proof of equivalence, although the paper says the means are "statistically equivalent".
- Pre-processing changes how the human-vs-AI comparison should be read. Pre-processing was kept to the minimum needed, but it still helped the model.
  quote: "After the application of any form of pre-processing, it essentially opens “Pandora’s box” as with enough pre-processing exceptional performance can be achieve despite it not being reflective of actual AI capabilities."
  where: section 2.3, p3
- The prompt-engineering recipe (Table 2): rewrite function definitions concisely (the example turns a prose definition into "definition of the function f (x) = x2 ∗ cos(2x)"), remove non-task text, add a preamble explaining the task, objectives and suggestions, mark the insertion point with "HERE HERE HERE", and elaborate post-task details. The raw condition (Table 1) already had a "# Please read this script and then complete the plot described by '::: Task :::' ..." instruction. The paper cites OpenAI's best-practices guide [11] for the claim that prompt engineering helps, and gives no ablation of which step mattered.
  where: p3-4

LIMITS
- Authors concede that pre-processing, and the extent of prompt engineering, shift the comparison from "AI ability" to "human-augmented AI". They say more step-by-step instructions might improve results further.
- Authors concede the student work may itself contain generative AI. This was against the course rules, but they "can't rule this out".
- Not shown:
  - No ablation of the individual prompt-engineering steps.
  - Only one model snapshot per tier, with no temperature or sampling settings reported.
  - Only 10 submissions per AI category. Failed or blank outputs were discarded and regenerated in a while loop, so there is survivorship bias. The failure rate is not reported.
  - Only plot quality was graded (assert-based function cells were pre-filled with correct answers).
  - No comparison with other prompting methods such as chain of thought or few-shot.
- Statistics: t-tests are run on pooled marker scores, so n=300 data points are not independent (three markers per submission). No multiple-comparison correction is mentioned.
- Dated: the models are gpt-3.5-turbo and gpt-4-1106-preview (2023). The authors expect LLMs may soon outperform students.
- Student 91.9% vs 91.1% inconsistency (see above). "55 randomly selected" from 103 consenting students, with 50 used.
- Mixed group used 5 students' plots, 10 submissions.

BUILDS ON: OpenAI best practices for prompt engineering (June 2023) [11]; Feng et al. 2024 (pre-processing/input format affects GPT-4 performance) [10]; Chen et al. 2021 (Codex); Austin et al. 2021 (MBPP); Tian et al. 2023; Yeadon et al. 2024 (physics essays, humans could not tell AI from human) [5]; Dell'Acqua et al. 2023 on user involvement.

CODE: none in the paper. Code repo given: https://github.com/WillYeadon/AI-Exam-Completion

FIGURES (captions only, images not viewed)
- Fig 1 (p5): "Percent scores for each of the six categories of submission." It shows students on top, GPT-4 PE and Mixed close behind, and GPT-3.5 strictly worse than GPT-4.
- Fig 2 (p6): histogram of markers' assigned authorship against actual authorship over 300 assessed submissions.
- Fig 3 (p9): stacked histogram of scores by the three markers.

PROBLEMS: No extraction faults, apart from the minor 91.9/91.1 mismatch in the source itself. No embedded instructions found. Note for the note on evaluating prompts: this is a small single-course study. It is useful as an example of a before/after prompt comparison with blind grading and reported inter-rater reliability (ICC), but not as general evidence on prompt engineering.
